Advanced Usage
==============

This document covers some of Requests more advanced features.

.. _session-objects:

Session Objects
---------------

The Session object allows you to persist certain parameters across
requests. It also persists cookies across all requests made from the
Session instance, and will use ``urllib3``'s `connection pooling`_. So if
you're making several requests to the same host, the underlying TCP
connection will be reused, which can result in a significant performance
increase (see `HTTP persistent connection`_).

A Session object has all the methods of the main Requests API.

Let's persist some cookies across requests::

    s = requests.Session()

    s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')
    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')

    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"sessioncookie": "123456789"}}'


Sessions can also be used to provide default data to the request methods. This
is done by providing data to the properties on a Session object::

    s = requests.Session()
    s.auth = ('user', 'pass')
    s.headers.update({'x-test': 'true'})

    # both 'x-test' and 'x-test2' are sent
    s.get('https://httpbin.org/headers', headers={'x-test2': 'true'})


Any dictionaries that you pass to a request method will be merged with the
session-level values that are set. The method-level parameters override session
parameters.

Note, however, that method-level parameters will *not* be persisted across
requests, even if using a session. This example will only send the cookies
with the first request, but not the second::

    s = requests.Session()

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies={'from-my': 'browser'})
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"from-my": "browser"}}'

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {}}'


If you want to manually add cookies to your session, use the
:ref:`Cookie utility functions <api-cookies>` to manipulate
:attr:`Session.cookies <requests.Session.cookies>`.

Sessions can also be used as context managers::

    with requests.Session() as s:
        s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')

This will make sure the session is closed as soon as the ``with`` block is
exited, even if unhandled exceptions occurred.


.. admonition:: Remove a Value From a Dict Parameter

    Sometimes you'll want to omit session-level keys from a dict parameter. To
    do this, you simply set that key's value to ``None`` in the method-level
    parameter. It will automatically be omitted.

All values that are contained within a session are directly available to you.
See the :ref:`Session API Docs <sessionapi>` to learn more.

Request and Response Objects
----------------------------

Whenever a call is made to ``requests.get()`` and friends, you are doing two
major things. First, you are constructing a ``Request`` object which will be
sent off to a server to request or query some resource. Second, a ``Response``
object is generated once Requests gets a response back from the server.
The ``Response`` object contains all of the information returned by the server and
also contains the ``Request`` object you created originally. Here is a simple
request to get some very important information from Wikipedia's servers::

    >>> r = requests.get('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python')

If we want to access the headers the server sent back to us, we do this::

However, if we want to get the headers we sent the server, we simply access the

# Requests HTTP Client and Its Python Networking Ecosystem

The community is centered on Requests, an open-source Python HTTP client that connects a broad set of internal components, authentication mechanisms, transport features, dependencies, testing tools, documentation platforms, and distribution services. Requests supports HTTP and HTTPS communication, proxy routing, TLS verification, cookies, redirects, streaming, multipart uploads, response decoding, and Basic and Digest Authentication. It is hosted in the PSF GitHub namespace, documented through Read the Docs, distributed through PyPI, and released under the Apache-2.0 license. The surrounding ecosystem includes urllib3-related networking behavior, Charset Normalizer, optional SOCKS and Brotli support, Requests-Toolbelt, asynchronous integrations, and extensive test infrastructure. Requests is the dominant hub in the community, with relationships covering core modules, protocols, dependencies, documentation, packaging, tests, standards, and related projects. Its documented functionality spans request construction, sessions, adapters, response processing, authentication, cookies, redirects, uploads, streaming, and error handling. [Data: Entities (46, 47, 48, 49, 50); Relationships (407, 408, 409, 410, 411, +more)]

RequestsCookieJar is the default cookie-container implementation used by Requests sessions to store, persist, merge, set, retrieve, remove, and inspect cookies associated with HTTP requests and responses. Advanced Usage
==============

This document covers some of Requests more advanced features.

.. _session-objects:

Session Objects
---------------

The Session object allows you to persist certain parameters across
requests. It also persists cookies across all requests made from the
Session instance, and will use ``urllib3``'s `connection pooling`_. So if
you're making several requests to the same host, the underlying TCP
connection will be reused, which can result in a significant performance
increase (see `HTTP persistent connection`_).

A Session object has all the methods of the main Requests API.

Let's persist some cookies across requests::

    s = requests.Session()

    s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')
    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')

    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"sessioncookie": "123456789"}}'


Sessions can also be used to provide default data to the request methods. This
is done by providing data to the properties on a Session object::

    s = requests.Session()
    s.auth = ('user', 'pass')
    s.headers.update({'x-test': 'true'})

    # both 'x-test' and 'x-test2' are sent
    s.get('https://httpbin.org/headers', headers={'x-test2': 'true'})


Any dictionaries that you pass to a request method will be merged with the
session-level values that are set. The method-level parameters override session
parameters.

Note, however, that method-level parameters will *not* be persisted across
requests, even if using a session. This example will only send the cookies
with the first request, but not the second::

    s = requests.Session()

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies={'from-my': 'browser'})
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"from-my": "browser"}}'

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {}}'


If you want to manually add cookies to your session, use the
:ref:`Cookie utility functions <api-cookies>` to manipulate
:attr:`Session.cookies <requests.Session.cookies>`.

Sessions can also be used as context managers::

    with requests.Session() as s:
        s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')

This will make sure the session is closed as soon as the ``with`` block is
exited, even if unhandled exceptions occurred.


.. admonition:: Remove a Value From a Dict Parameter

    Sometimes you'll want to omit session-level keys from a dict parameter. To
    do this, you simply set that key's value to ``None`` in the method-level
    parameter. It will automatically be omitted.

All values that are contained within a session are directly available to you.
See the :ref:`Session API Docs <sessionapi>` to learn more.

.. _request-and-response-objects:

Request and Response Objects
----------------------------

Whenever a call is made to ``requests.get()`` and friends, you are doing two
major things. First, you are constructing a ``Request`` object which will be
sent off to a server to request or query some resource. Second, a ``Response``
object is generated once Requests gets a response back from the server.
The ``Response`` object contains all of the information returned by the server and
also contains the ``Request`` object you created originally. Here is a simple
request to get some very important information from Wikipedia's servers::

    >>> r = requests.get('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python')

Advanced Usage
==============

This document covers some of Requests more advanced features.

.. _session-objects:

Session Objects
---------------

The Session object allows you to persist certain parameters across
requests. It also persists cookies across all requests made from the
Session instance, and will use ``urllib3``'s `connection pooling`_. So if
you're making several requests to the same host, the underlying TCP
connection will be reused, which can result in a significant performance
increase (see `HTTP persistent connection`_).

A Session object has all the methods of the main Requests API.

Let's persist some cookies across requests::

    s = requests.Session()

    s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')
    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')

    print(r.text)
    # '{""cookies"": {""sessioncookie"": ""123456789""}}'


Sessions can also be used to provide default data to the request methods. This
is done by providing data to the properties on a Session object::

    s = requests.Session()
    s.auth = ('user', 'pass')
    s.headers.update({'x-test': 'true'})

    # both 'x-test' and 'x-test2' are sent
    s.get('https://httpbin.org/headers', headers={'x-test2': 'true'})


Any dictionaries that you pass to a request method will be merged with the
session-level values that are set. The method-level parameters override session
parameters.

Note, however, that method-level parameters will *not* be persisted across
requests, even if using a session. This example will only send the cookies
with the first request, but not the second::

    s = requests.Session()

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies={'from-my': 'browser'})
    print(r.text)
    # '{""cookies"": {""from-my"": ""browser""}}'

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')
    print(r.text)
    # '{""cookies"": {}}'


If you want to manually add cookies to your session, use the
:ref:`Cookie utility functions <api-cookies>` to manipulate
:attr:`Session.cookies <requests.Session.cookies>`.

Sessions can also be used as context managers::

    with requests.Session() as s:
        s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')

This will make sure the session is closed as soon as the ``with`` block is
exited, even if unhandled exceptions occurred.


.. admonition:: Remove a Value From a Dict Parameter

    Sometimes you'll want to omit session-level keys from a dict parameter. To
    do this, you simply set that key's value to ``None`` in the method-level
    parameter. It will automatically be omitted.

All values that are contained within a session are directly available to you.
See the :ref:`Session API Docs <sessionapi>` to learn more.

.. _request-and-response-objects:

Request and Response Objects
----------------------------

Whenever a call is made to ``requests.get()`` and friends, you are doing two
major things. First, you are constructing a ``Request`` object which will be
sent off to a server to request or query some resource. Second, a ``Response``
object is generated once Requests gets a response back from the server.
The ``Response`` object contains all of the information returned by the server and
also contains the ``Request`` object you created originally. Here is a simple
request to get some very important information from Wikipedia's servers::

    >>> r = requests.get('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python')

If we want to access the headers the server sent back to us, we do this::

    >>> r.headers
    {'content-length': '56170', 'x-content-type-options': 'nosniff', 'x-cache':
    'HIT from cp1006.eqiad.wmnet, MISS from cp1010.eqiad.wmnet', 'content-encoding':
    'gzip', 'age': '3080', 'content-language': 'en', 'vary': 'Accept-Encoding,Cookie',
    'server': 'Apache', 'last-modified': 'Wed, 13 Jun 2012 01:33:50 GMT',
    'connection': 'close', 'cache-control': 'private, s-maxage=0, max-age=0,
    must-revalidate', 'date': 'Thu, 14 Jun 2012 12:59:39 GMT', 'content-type':
    'text/html; charset=UTF-8', 'x-cache-lookup': 'HIT from cp1006.eqiad.wmnet:3128,
    MISS from cp1010.eqiad.wmnet:80'}

However, if we want to get the headers we sent the server, we simply access the
request, and then the request's headers::

    >>> r.request.headers
    {'Accept-Encoding': 'identity, deflate, compress, gzip',
    'Accept': '*/*', 'User-Agent': 'python-requests/1.2.0'}

.. _prepared-requests:

Prepared Requests
-----------------

Whenever you receive a :class:`Response <requests.Response>` object
from an API call or a Session call, the ``request`` attribute is actually the
``PreparedRequest`` that was used. In some cases you may wish to do some extra
work to the body or headers (or anything else really) before sending a
request. The simple recipe for this is the following::

    from requests import Request, Session

    s = Session()

    req = Request('POST', url, data=data, headers=headers)
    prepped = req.prepare()

# Requests HTTP Client and Its Python Networking Ecosystem

SESSION is a Requests library client object that manages persistent state and configuration while sending multiple HTTP and HTTPS requests. It stores and applies cookies, headers, authentication, proxy settings, hooks, environment settings, certificates, and TLS verification options. SESSION creates and mounts HTTPAdapter instances to contact HTTP and HTTPS URLs, maintaining separate connection pools when TLS configurations differ and providing connection pooling for efficient reuse. It prepares and sends requests, including prepared requests, resolves redirect chains subject to configured redirect limits, and manages the adapters used for network communication. SESSION also supports pickling and serves as the central mechanism for maintaining consistent request behavior across a series of HTTP operations.

Requests cookies provides the cookie-management functionality used by the test suite. It includes the `RequestsCookieJar` cookie-jar implementation, along with utilities for converting between cookie jars, dictionaries, and morsels. It also supports copying cookie jars and generating HTTP cookie headers.

RequestsCookieJar is the default cookie-container implementation used by Requests sessions to store, persist, merge, set, retrieve, remove, and inspect cookies associated with HTTP requests and responses. It extends Python’s `http.cookiejar.CookieJar` while implementing a dictionary-like `MutableMapping` interface, allowing dictionary-style `__getitem__`, `__setitem__`, and `__delitem__` operations as well as compatibility with dictionary-based cookie insertion and updates. RequestsCookieJar supports copying while preserving both its cookie policy and contents, and it can be serialized with pickle by excluding its unpickleable `_cookies_lock` from the serialized state and restoring the lock afterward. For cookie lookup, it uses `_find_no_duplicates` when strict retrieval is required and `_find` when it may arbitrarily choose among cookies with conflicting names. It therefore combines standard cookie-jar behavior with convenient mapping semantics for managing cookies throughout Requests sessions.

Advanced Usage
==============

This document covers some of Requests more advanced features.

.. _session-objects:

Session Objects
---------------

The Session object allows you to persist certain parameters across
requests. It also persists cookies across all requests made from the
Session instance, and will use ``urllib3``'s `connection pooling`_. So if
you're making several requests to the same host, the underlying TCP
connection will be reused, which can result in a significant performance
increase (see `HTTP persistent connection`_).

A Session object has all the methods of the main Requests API.

Let's persist some cookies across requests::

    s = requests.Session()

    s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')
    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')

    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"sessioncookie": "123456789"}}'


Sessions can also be used to provide default data to the request methods. This
is done by providing data to the properties on a Session object::

    s = requests.Session()
    s.auth = ('user', 'pass')
    s.headers.update({'x-test': 'true'})

    # both 'x-test' and 'x-test2' are sent
    s.get('https://httpbin.org/headers', headers={'x-test2': 'true'})


Any dictionaries that you pass to a request method will be merged with the
session-level values that are set. The method-level parameters override session
parameters.

Note, however, that method-level parameters will *not* be persisted across
requests, even if using a session. This example will only send the cookies
with the first request, but not the second::

    s = requests.Session()

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies', cookies={'from-my': 'browser'})
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {"from-my": "browser"}}'

    r = s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')
    print(r.text)
    # '{"cookies": {}}'


If you want to manually add cookies to your session, use the
:ref:`Cookie utility functions <api-cookies>` to manipulate
:attr:`Session.cookies <requests.Session.cookies>`.

Sessions can also be used as context managers::

    with requests.Session() as s:
        s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/sessioncookie/123456789')

This will make sure the session is closed as soon as the ``with`` block is
exited, even if unhandled exceptions occurred.


.. admonition:: Remove a Value From a Dict Parameter

    Sometimes you'll want to omit session-level keys from a dict parameter. To
    do this, you simply set that key's value to ``None`` in the method-level
    parameter. It will automatically be omitted.

All values that are contained within a session are directly available to you.
See the :ref:`Session API Docs <sessionapi>` to learn more.

Request and Response Objects
----------------------------

Whenever a call is made to ``requests.get()`` and friends, you are doing two
major things. First, you are constructing a ``Request`` object which will be
sent off to a server to request or query some resource. Second, a ``Response``
object is generated once Requests gets a response back from the server.
The ``Response`` object contains all of the information returned by the server and
also contains the ``Request`` object you created originally. Here is a simple
request to get some very important information from Wikipedia's servers::
